habit: Do one small thing every day to reduce your stress
blurb: Stress puts the brakes on progress. A few minutes a day makes a real difference.

1.p: For the next two weeks, I challenge you to reduce your stress.
A common theme I see amongst those with high stress levels is a lack of results when trying to change their body. Stress holds us back from being the best that we can be.

In a very similar way to poor sleep, it can put the brakes on progress, even if training and nutrition are spot-on. Of course, we all suffer stress at some point in our lives. We are involved in regular stressful life situations, including exhausting work schedules.

Stress is a burden on the body, and if it becomes chronically elevated and prolonged, we can end up massively fatigued and run down. That’s when it can put a halt to any body composition changes. What we don’t always realise is the potential damage stress is doing to the inside of our bodies and how it affects our health.

1.h: How can I personalise this habit?

1.p: Assess the stressful areas of your life. Family, friends, career and money issues can all be stressful issues at times, and it’s important to manage these as much as possible. Find the root cause(s) of stress and then put a simple daily habit into place to reduce, manage or eliminate them.
I highly recommend practicing the art of daily meditation for this habit. It is one of the most effective ways at reducing overall daily stress levels.
Other habits could be taking more regular breaks at work, or getting more exercise in daily, or socialising more with friends and family.

Remember to relax, laugh, sleep and have sex as much as possible, as these reduce stress levels in the body. Reduce the main stressors in your lifestyle and remember not to take life too seriously all the time.

1.h: How can I make this habit easy?

1.p: The first step is to scale the habit to something you are 90-100% confident you can do for 6 days of the week. Have one day off per week from completing the habit.

1.h: What can I piggyback off of?

1.p: I highly recommend finding a trigger in the time you choose to meditate. I would however recommend you start meditating in the mornings Why? Because if it’s later in the day, it can usually get pushed back when other things get in the way. Choose a trigger that’s already in your daily routine that you’re going to tie the habit to. Examples: waking up, drinking your first cup of coffee, eating breakfast, brushing teeth, showering, using bathroom in the morning, opening your computer for the first time, arriving at work.
TO DO: Create your personal version of the habit to commit to this challenge!

1.h: Here’s a template

1.p: I am 90-100% confident that I will [insert habit] for 6 days a week after I [insert what you’re going to piggyback off of].

1.h: Here’s an example

1.p: I am 90-100% confident that I will complete 2 minutes of meditation for 6 days a week after I eat my breakfast.
P.S. Don’t worry about making this perfect. I’ll help you adjust.

li: Find a quiet spot. Sometimes early morning is best, before others in your house might be awake. Others for example might find a spot in a park or on the beach on their lunch break. It really doesn’t matter where — as long as you can sit without being bothered for a couple minutes.

Sit comfortably. I personally like to lie on my bed, but anything that you find comfortable will do. You can for example place a pillow on the floor and rest your back against the wall or find a suitable chair.

Start with just 2 minutes. This is a really important point. You’ll find it much easier to start this way, and forming a habit with a small start like this is a method much more likely to succeed. Try expanding it to 5 minutes if you can do the 2-minute meditation for 7 straight days, then 7 minutes if you can do it for 14 straight days, then 10 minutes if you can stick to it for 21 straight days, and 15 if you can do a full month. But don’t increase your meditation time unless you didn’t miss a day the previous week.

Focus on your body and breath. First notice your body — what position are you in? Are your ears, shoulders and hips aligned? Now check in with your breath. As you breathe in, follow your breath in through your nostrils, then into your throat, then into your lungs and belly. Sit straight, keep your eyes open but looking at the ground and with a soft focus. If you want to close your eyes, that’s fine. As you breathe out, follow your breath out back into the world. If it helps, count ... one breath in, two breath out, three breath in, four breath out ... when you get to 10, start over. If you lose track, start over. If you find your mind wandering (and you will), just pay attention to your mind wandering, then bring it gently back to your breath. Repeat this process for the two minutes you meditate. You won’t be very good at it at first, most likely, but you’ll get better with practice.

2.p: And that’s it. It’s a very simple practice, but it’s a great way to form the meditation habit and then experience all the benefit it brings. We will get to some more advanced stuff along the way

3.p: It’s fair to assume you currently have some stress in your life. It’s important to know what we can do nutritionally to support our health and reduce negative impacts from stress. I’ll outline some of the key points to consider below:
In times of stress your body is burning through more carbohydrates for energy. It’s therefore common for those under stress to experience low blood sugar levels, as demand for glucose is higher.

This can result in hypoglycaemia, or at the very least, to increased cravings for sugar. Those with high stress levels are typically on a constant blood sugar rollercoaster and always looking for their next sugar fix. On top of this, they rely on stimulants such as coffee and sodas to see them throughout the day.
These uncontrollable food urges are likely to cause overeating, as the body constantly strives for homeostasis to balance blood sugar levels. And that overeating generally leads to weight gain.
It is important for those with a sweet tooth to eat regularly throughout the day, with consistent meal timings. The goal should be to never go hypoglycaemic.

Meals should be nutritionally balanced with adequate protein, fats and carbs from high quality food sources. Sugary food, caffeine and alcohol should be limited as these have a negative effect on blood sugar levels.

Intermittent fasting (IF) has become one of the most debated modern nutrition protocols, and rightfully so because it breaks a lot of rules. For decades we have been told to eat every 2-3 hours and to eat breakfast upon waking to ‘kick-start’ our metabolism for optimal body composition and health.
IF goes against this by reducing meal frequency and delaying breakfast. Many fasting protocols suggest eating less during the day and feasting at night.
Fasting isn’t a tool I’d recommend for those with high stress levels as it puts even more pressure on the adrenals to maintain a level of blood glucose.

When recommending IF protocols it’s important for the user to be in a good state of health, already eating whole unprocessed foods, getting sufficient sleep, managing stress and exercising well. It should therefore be used as an addition to an already effective and consistent training and nutrition strategy.

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred source of energy, and this becomes more apparent during times of stress. To provide the energy to support recovery from the stress, follow a higher carbohydrate diet.
A low calorie intake during stressful times or recovery from high stress will only heighten the depletion of glycogen, breakdown of muscle tissue and put more demand on the adrenals.
Therefore you should look to eat at ‘calorie maintenance’ level or a slight surplus during stressful times.

5.p: Sometimes the stress we experience daily is due to our own thoughts.

Thinking habits can be very hard to change, because we’re usually not aware we’re doing them, and they’re harder to notice than physical habits. It’s easier to see when you’re eating junk food than when you’re thinking negative things about yourself.
So the key, as always, is forming an awareness of the habit and triggers.
Keep a journal, write brief entry into it when you notice these thoughts. You might spend a few minutes in the morning just watching your thoughts, noticing patterns.
It’s important to note that this habit wont change overnight, but is something that could take months or years to slowly improve.
A good replacement habit is to notice your negative thoughts (about yourself, others, life), and stay with that feeling for a while.

8.p: If all went well last week, and you didn’t struggle or skip the habit for more than a day, I recommend that you lengthen the habit this week. If you’ve struggled, keep it the same as last week or make it even easier.
For example, if you’ve been doing 2 minutes of meditation daily, then extend that to 4 minutes this week.
Or if you’ve been getting more exercise by walking for 10 minutes on your lunch break at work, try extending that to 15 minutes this week.
Never make too big an adjustment so that it becomes too difficult.
This slow change process of expanding the habit a little at a time helps overcome the resistance of the mind to change and discomfort.
Each step isn’t difficult, so your mind doesn’t rebel much. Gradually the habit becomes your new normal and you can expand a bit more, pushing your comfort zone a little at a time.

9.p: I’ve found exercise to be one of the best ways to reduce stress (alongside mediation). Ironically, it can be hard to start exercising if you’re tired and stressed, but I’ve always felt a lot better after exercise, so it’s worth putting some effort into starting.
A fast walk, a good run, some strength training, a swim or bike ride, or playing a sport are all great ideas.

Not only does exercise reduce stress, but it helps you to sleep better at night. While it’s good to exercise regularly, it’s also best to have at least one or two days break from higher intensity exercise too.

10.p: Sometimes you’re stressed or overwhelmed because there’s too much going on in your life or too much information coming in.
To make this more manageable, make a list of all you have going on right now.
Now see if you can eliminate or put a hold on a few of them – simply send an email or make a call and tell people you can’t work or do this right now.
Make a short list of three to five tasks you can actually work on today, and focus on the first item only. One thing at a time.

Also remember to take breaks from these tasks. Get away from the computer, and take a walk. This is the best way to deal with stress – find ways to de-stress during the day. Stretch. Move around. Get some fresh air. Talk to someone in real life. Take a hot bath or shower if that’s possible.
Remind yourself: all that you have going on...doesn’t matter that much. At the end of the day, life will go on.

11.p: We’re almost at the end of the ‘Reduce your stress’ habit challenge.
As you prepare to move onto the next habit challenge, you’ll want to put this current habit into ‘habit maintenance mode.’
This is a way of continuing it with less of a focus.

By now, the habit should start to become more automatic if you’ve been at least a little consistent. You don’t need reminders to start the habit, and it’s feeling a bit easier, more part of your ‘normal.’
So as you begin to move your focus to the next habit challenge, all you want to do is not forget about this habit. You don’t need to keep track of it every day, as long as things are going well.

But every few days, pause and reflect on this habit and check in to see that everything is still going well. Maybe once a week, use one of our Sunday reflection sessions to assess whether you have any obstacles around this habit, need to make adjustments, learned anything new.
After a while, you need to reflect on the habit less often, as it becomes ingrained in your life.
Stay focused this weekend and remember to have some fun in the process!

blurb: Four weeks alcohol-free — and the science of what it’s really doing to your sleep, training and fat loss.

1.h: Alcohol is funny

1.p: Not HA HA HAH funny…even though you may think so after you’ve had a few.
It’s funny because it is an ever-increasing part of most people’s social lives and is one of the most commonly consumed and socially acceptable drugs in the world.
In spite of this, it seems to also be at odds with our health, mental well-being and (the reason you’re likely reading this) our physical appearance and performance.
We have no NEED to consume alcohol but most of us have a strong DESIRE to do so.

For most it’s the catalyst that causes a shift from sensible, button-down family life to a weekend of carnage and debauchery and many people at some point in their lives rely on it as an on-demand source of stress relief and release.

2.p: Alcohol affects hormones, blood sugar, and gut health. Knowing the effects can help reinforce your commitment.
Alcohol is a Macronutrient.
A WHAT?!
Yep, it’s a Macronutrient.
That means that like Protein, Carbohydrates and Fats, it contains calories for every gram you consume.

Alcohol contains 7 calories per gramme, nearly as calorie dense as fat. However, the thermic effects of digestion do suggest that the net usable calories we receive from consuming alcohol are likely lower than this.
Tomorrow we'll look at how alcohol can actually impact the things that we care about when it comes to getting stronger and fitter.

3.p: A study by Siler, Neese, and Hellerstein found that just 24g of alcohol—roughly one large glass of wine or a pint of beer—is enough to stop your body from burning fat for a while.
Why? When your liver breaks down alcohol, it makes acetate, which your body uses for energy instead of fat. This blocks fat burning (lipolysis) and shifts how your body uses fuel.
So yep—just one drink can put fat loss on pause.
Pass the water.

Sonko and his team found that alcohol temporarily slows fat burning after a meal, but things return to normal once the alcohol is processed. Like carbs, alcohol spares fat (it’s used for energy instead), and it only leads to fat gain if you’re eating more calories than your body needs.
So yes—it still comes down to calories in vs. calories out.
Simple, right?

4.p: Other Effects (aka Why You End Up Raiding the Fridge)
Alright, quick science moment—stick with me.

When you drink alcohol, your body breaks it down through a few chemical steps (ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetate). During this process, your body shifts gears and stops making new glucose (sugar) from stored sources.
Your blood sugar drops, and you get super hungry. Hello, late-night cheesy chips.
So, on top of slowing fat loss, alcohol can make you eat more without even realizing it—which can undo all your hard work, even if you're “good” the rest of the week.

5.p: We have two sides to examine here.

li: One is the impact on MPS (muscle protein synthesis) and the other is
The impact on Testosterone (with downstream effects for muscle and strength gain)
Muscle & Strength Gain

5.p: ClarksonPM1, ReichsmanF.gave 10 women alcohol PRIOR to exercise and tested protein leakage, damage,force production and range of motion. They found NO difference in the alcohol and non-alcohol groups.
In summary, drinking alcohol PRIOR to training won’t exaggerate the tissue damage you accumulate during the session.

Parr and Camera tested 8 active men by giving them either alcohol, whey and alcohol or carbs and alcohol, accounting for total calorie load of each. Muscle biopsies were taken 2 and 8 hours post exercise.
They concluded that muscle protein synthesis was suppressed, even when combining alcohol with protein.
In summary, the bad news is that even if we drink down our beer with a protein shake, protein synthesis IS decreased following alcohol ingestion.
So, no…slamming a shake with Tequila won’t save us.

6.p: PoulsenMB1, JakobsenJ, AagaardNK, Andersen H tested 19 healthy men and women to see if alcohol ingestion impacted Isokinetic and isometric muscle strength and endurance were impacted (in other words, how strong they were and stuff).
“a single episode of moderate alcohol intoxication (1,4 g/l) does not impair motor performance, and no accelerated exercise-induced muscle damage is seen”.
In summary, alcohol may impact protein synthesis and our recovery, but in terms of how much weight you can lift or how long you can run for, it ain’t no thang!
Another study gave 19 people (men and women) 3–4 drinks a day for 6 weeks.

li: Results:
Testosterone in men dropped by ~7%
No effect on testosterone in women
DHEAS (a hormone linked to mood and metabolism) increased in both
Keep in mind:

6.p: 3–4 drinks every day is a lot — way more than most people typically drink.
Alcohol might take a small shot at testosterone levels in men.
Ladies, you're in the clear. Guys… not so much.

li: Reduces muscle protein synthesis after exercise, it’s safe to assume that this is only while alcohol is being metabolised.
Alcohol doesn’t appear to have a significant effect on strength, endurance or power output.
Alcohol does decrease testosterone in men, this seems to be a relatively small decrease from large doses. Again, this is likely to be only on a short-term basis.

8.p: If you’re reading this, I think you’ll have likely experienced that sleep can drastically affect not only how you feel but also things like:

li: Training performance
Perceived recovery and soreness
Hunger and food cravings
Emotional wellbeing
Energy and willpower

8.p: In other words, it’s pretty damn important.
Moreover, as our work life balance is constantly tested by an increasingly connected world, chances are you aren’t currently benefiting from the luxury of 8+ hours per night.
With this, we need to consider how we can get the most bang for our snoozy bucks.

9.h: Alcohol & Sleep: The Science Bit (Made Simple)

9.p: Researchers in Japan studied how alcohol affects sleep and heart rate. They looked at how alcohol messes with your nervous system while you’re sleeping.
Quick recap:
Your parasympathetic system helps you rest and recover.
Your sympathetic system keeps you alert and stressed.
Good sleep = more parasympathetic, less stress.
They used heart rate variability to track this.
They gave 10 guys low, medium, or high doses of alcohol before bed.
Here’s what happened with the high doses (think 3–5 drinks depending on your size):

li: 👉 Less REM (dream) sleep
👉 More stress response (higher heart rate)
👉 Worse recovery

9.p: So yep—alcohol seriously messes with your sleep, even if you don’t feel drunk.
And no, it doesn’t take a wild night out to do it.

10.p: Now we can definitively say that doses of 1g/kg of alcohol:

li: For a 90kg man = 4-5 pints OR 3-4 glasses of wine
For a 60kg woman = 3-4 pints OR 2-3 glasses of wine

10.p: Of course, this depends on strength of the wine and beer but the above wouldn’t be a crazy night on the tiles for most people and yet with these doses, noticeable decreases in sleep quality were noted.

li: More time in stage 1 sleep and less time in deeper stages of sleep.
More wake ups
Less parasympathetic activity and a lower restorative benefit to sleep
Higher heart rate

11.p: So, now we know the details. My typical pet peeve is with articles that just spew loads of number and data at you with no succinct way of managing this information and integrating it into your life.
While doing research for this, Came across something I like called the 3i's Formula. (See picture)
What this says in short is that in order to succeed, we need a combination and integration of information, integration and Individual Accountability.

In other words, it’s nice to know the ins and outs of the science as it relates to alcohol and how it affects our progress. However, if we just become one of those people who just sits and reads PubMed without taking action, it isn’t going to help us AT ALL with our progress.
So, the first step, we’ve covered. We need information that is simple (so that we can actually use it) and relevant (to us, our lives and our goals).

The next piece of this puzzle is integration. In other words, how do we go about actually using this information inside of our worlds. This, in my opinion is where most coaches and articles fail and what I’m going to cover next.
And individual accountability…well if you want more of that, just send me a message.

12.p: Consuming alcohol for the purposes of fat loss, muscle gain and strength will impact us in the following ways:

li: Temporarily prevents fat metabolism while alcohol is converted to Acetate.

Provides an additional source of calories outside of carbs, protein and fat that we need to somehow track and account for. Alcohol still adheres to the laws of thermodynamics despite what online gurus may have you believe.
Due to the methods of metabolism, . Priming the canvas for overeating.

12.p: We (obviously) experience lowered inhibition and discipline. Combined with low blood sugar, we’re more likely to overeat on days we drink.

li: Drinking PRIOR to training hasn’t been shown to accelerate or exaggerate muscle damage, however, this likely won’t lead to the most productive training session.

Even when combining alcohol with protein post, 2 and 8 hours post workout, muscle protein synthesis is suppressed. Not only will this hamper our recovery but also the training effect we receive from a training session.
Alcohol does not seem to have any negative impact on force generation and muscular endurance.

13.p: Alcohol when consumed in relatively large amounts and over a sustained period does slightly negatively impact testosterone levels in men.

li: Even a few beers or wines can worsen our sleep depth and quality
Heart rate and nervous system activity are impacted and therefore recovery is damaged
For most alcohol doesn’t equate to a warm, bath and early night.

14.p: (Like when you’re so BIG & STRONG that you smash the champagne glass….gains)

15.p: This is what we call the consistency funnel and again, serves as a backbone within our coaching programs. I find it helps to explain concepts like this visually.
You’re probably already familiar with this BUT what we’re saying here is that in order to achieve success in any fitness pursuit we need to apply consistency to the basic stuff.
We can fuss and faff over the details all we want but these three key things are what ACTUALLY drives progress.
Calories, in line with our goal. EVERY DAY.
Planned training volume completed. EVERY WEEK.
Over 35 hours of sleep. EVERY… you get the picture.

16.p: So, we need to view alcohol through this lens and yep…it makes EVERY SINGLE ONE of the above more difficult to achieve.
What this says in short is that if we drink such that we violate:

li: Our weekly total training volume
Our weekly total sleep volume
To the extent that we start to touch on levels that may begin to affect testosterone

16.p: The alcohol is a bad idea.
Yep, sorry to be the bearer of bad news but if you’re going your calorie targets by 1000s each week because you can’t control your marginal propensity for PINTS, you’ll probably get fat…
…don’t hate the player, hate the game.

17.h: Things are pretty simple here. There are 2 potentials scenarios

17.p: We work alcohol into our existing daily calories
We accept that we’re likely to overshoot calories on the day we drink and so account for it across a week or month.
A little bit of honesty here can really shed some light on your reality too.
Some people just bloody love getting wrecked and smashing pints (LADS LADS LADS).
Some people drink to ease social anxiety.
Some people drink to squash criticism and social pressure, just trying to fit in.
If we aren’t really clear on what it is we’re actually trying to get out of drinking then we aren’t able to plan effectively for it.

18.h: Why exactly is it that you drink? (continued)

li: What effect are you looking for?

18.p: If you’re looking to get really drunk, just be honest. Maybe you’re just looking to fit in with your friends and you absolutely HATE hangovers? Both are fine, all that matters is that you’re honest with yourself.

li: How often & HOW MUCH do you currently drink?

18.p: This is probably going to be pretty painful for some people. It requires that you take a very, very honest look at your current situation and examine how much you’re currently drinking, and how often. Again, if you’re downing a bottle of wine every night after work, stop lying about it!
Get crystal clear on your current reality and why you drink.
Why does this matter? Simply because the more we change from your norm right out of the gate, the harder it will be to stick to.

19.p: The Day before and the day after.
There are obvious consequences to alcohol consumption that WOULD impact the quality of our training the following day that should not be ignored:

li: Dehydration
Reduced motor control and co-ordination (aka still drunk. Yes, I've seen it way more ofter in my gym then you would think!)
Less motivation and resilience (aka feeling bloody awful)
Increased injury risk
Seems to be a pretty strong argument for not drinking and then going training the day after, right?
Well, what if we train first and THEN drink? We get:
Less calories from protein and carbohydrates to fuel and support training
Less sleep duration and quality following the training session
Protein synthesis impact
Potential for DOMS from the session are worse and last longer

19.p: However, to me there is one argument that sticks out above the others and that is the potential and risk of injury.

20.p: How Alcohol increases our risk of injury.

If we boil success in anything gym related down to consistency then we can say that the person who can continue to train for their goal over the longest period is likely to experience the best results.
Nothing kills consistency like a nice, juicy injury!
Training AFTER a night or day of drinking significantly increases your risk of injury and therefore, damaging your progress WAY beyond just the next 24-48 hours.

Alcohol consumption can increase the risk of injuries during training by impairing physical abilities like coordination, balance, and reaction time, and hindering recovery. It can also lead to dehydration, which further compromises performance and increases the likelihood of injury.
Protein synthesis is also lower over the subsequent day.

li: Here's a more detailed look on the impact of your Physical Abilities:
Impaired Coordination and Balance:

20.p: Alcohol negatively affects motor skills, coordination, and balance, making it harder to perform exercises safely and effectively.
Reduced reaction time can make it difficult to react to unexpected situations or movements during training, increasing the risk of accidents.
Alcohol can impair vision and judgment, potentially leading to missteps or poor decisions that result in injury.

li: Impact on Recovery:
Dehydration:

20.p: Alcohol is a diuretic, meaning it increases urination and can lead to dehydration.Dehydration can negatively affect performance and recovery, making muscles more susceptible to injury.
Alcohol can interfere with the body's natural healing processes, potentially prolonging the recovery time for injuries.
Alcohol can cause blood vessels to dilate, leading to increased swelling and bleeding around injuries, which can also slow down recovery.
Alcohol can interfere with protein synthesis and muscle repair, which are essential for muscle growth and recovery after training.

21.p: Remember, from the above, we know that even fairly moderate doses of alcohol impact your sleep.
Whenever a client has issues with sleep one of the first things I suggest is to ritualise and normalise their wake time.
When you wake up at the same time every day…YES…EVERY day, there is just something magical that seems to happen to your days and nights.
You start to feel sleepy at the same time in the evening and falling asleep is much easier.
You tend to start feeling hungry at the same time of the day.
Your performance when training is more reliable.
Honestly, when compared to a sporadic sleep schedule, making a ritual the time you wake up can create night and day results.

Now, of course, alcohol does pose quite a threat to this. We get in at 3am Saturday night, don’t wake up until gone midday on Sunday and then try to get to bed by 11pm for our normal Monday morning routine again…it isn’t going to happen.
This can obviously then create a cascade effect where our sleep is out of whack for the rest of the week…all because of a few beers!

We know that alcohol damages sleep depth and quality from the data. Unfortunately, aside from standard sleep hygiene advice (dark cold room, relax before bed etc) there isn’t all that much we can do to mitigate and remove the downsides if you drink. The best approach is to just eliminate the obvious risk factors for a bad night’s sleep (alcohol).

22.p: 3 weeks down – amazing. You’ve hit a key milestone.
Psychologists say it takes around 21 days to form a new habit, and that’s exactly where you are. What once felt unfamiliar or difficult might now feel... surprisingly normal.

li: Take a moment to check in:
How’s your energy?
How’s your sleep?
What’s your mood like?
How do you feel in your body?

22.p: Chances are, you’re feeling mentally clearer, more in control, and physically stronger than you did at the start. That’s no accident — it’s the result of the choices you’ve made, day after day.
You’re reclaiming your power, reshaping your habits, and proving what you’re capable of.
Keep going — the next week is where the real confidence starts to kick in.

23.p: Alcohol is everywhere. It’s at birthdays, weddings, BBQs, office parties, first dates, Friday nights, brunch, book club — you name it. It’s so normalized that not drinking can feel like the unusual choice.
But let’s be clear: just because something is common, doesn’t mean it’s good for you — or necessary.
You’re doing something powerful: challenging a cultural norm. You’re choosing presence over numbness, health over habit, clarity over conformity.
That takes self-awareness. It takes strength.
This challenge isn’t just about cutting out alcohol. It’s about standing up for yourself in a world that often encourages the opposite.
And that’s something to be proud of.

24.p: Alcohol isn’t just costly to your health — it hits your wallet too.
Whether it’s a few glasses of wine at home or rounds at the pub, those small spends add up fast.

li: Go ahead — pull out your calculator (or your bank app) and do a quick tally:
How much would you normally spend on alcohol in a week?
Multiply that by 3 (you’ve gone over 3 weeks alcohol-free!)
Surprised?

24.p: That’s money you didn’t drink — and it’s yours to spend, save, or invest however you want.
What feels like a meaningful reward?

24.h: A massage? New gym gear? A weekend getaway? A savings boost?

24.p: This isn’t about replacing one dopamine hit with another — it’s about recognizing your effort and choosing to celebrate in a way that aligns with your goals.
You’ve saved money and built discipline.

25.p: Worried that you're missing the craic in the pub? House party? Or other socially lubricated gathering?

You’re not ‘missing out.’ You've been there before and know exactly what happens. And while it is good to meet friends and catch up, why not save that for special occasions? You want to make going out and drinking something that happens only a few times a year.
You’re not waking up groggy. You’re not replaying conversations with regret. You’re not spending Sundays recovering instead of living.
Instead, you’re waking up clear-headed, aligned with your goals, and fully present in your life. You’re more connected to your choices, your values, and your body.
That’s not missing out — that’s showing up.

Every time you choose not to drink, you’re strengthening your self-respect. You’re proving that fun, confidence, and connection don’t depend on alcohol. That you don’t need a substance to loosen up or “fit in.”
You’re in control — of your energy, your time, your mood, your habits.
And that kind of power? That’s rare. That’s bold. That’s yours.

26.p: If you go drinking out every weekend...
Let’s be honest: when you drink enough to wake up hungover, you’re not just losing a few hours — you’re losing the whole day.
You don’t feel like moving. Your brain’s foggy. You’re reaching for junk food, skipping the workout, avoiding sunlight, canceling plans, and telling yourself, “I’ll get back on track tomorrow.”
But tomorrow was supposed to be today.
Week after week, that adds up to 52 days a year — nearly two full months of wasted potential, energy, and momentum.

li: Imagine what you could do with those days:
Early hikes instead of greasy takeaways
Journaling instead of doom scrolling
Connection instead of regret
Progress instead of pause

26.p: Every hangover is like robbing your future self of a day they could’ve used for something better.

27.p: Let’s talk about stress and drinking.
For many people, reaching for a drink isn’t really about the alcohol — it’s about relief. A way to take the edge off after a long day, soothe anxiety, or create a pause in the chaos.
It’s totally normal to crave comfort when stress hits.
But here’s the catch: alcohol doesn’t actually reduce stress. It just numbs it… temporarily. And when it wears off? The stress is still there — sometimes even worse.
The good news? You can train your body and brain to respond differently.
The first step is finding healthier ways to downshift when tension rises.

27.h: Here are a few quick wins

27.p: Go for a walk. Movement helps discharge nervous energy and clears your mind.
Play music you love. Let it shift your mood and energy.
Try breathwork. Even just 60 seconds of slow, deep breathing can reset your nervous system.
Write it out. A brain dump in a journal can release mental pressure.
Connect. Call someone who makes you feel safe and seen.
Stress will always be part of life. But how you respond to it? That’s where your power lies.

27.h: So today, when the urge hits, pause and ask

27.p: What am I really needing right now — and what’s one way I can meet that need without alcohol?
You’ve got options. Choose one that serves you.

28.p: You’ve made it through — not just without alcohol, but with insight, strength, and intention.

li: Over the last few weeks, you’ve learned so much about how alcohol truly impacts your body:
How it disrupts fat loss and blocks recovery
How it interferes with sleep and derails hormones
How it affects your training, energy, mood, and hunger
And how easily it can hijack your progress — even when everything else is on point
But more importantly, you’ve gained something even more valuable:
You now know how to:
Handle cravings when stress hits
Say no in social settings with confidence
Create rituals and rewards that actually serve you
Stay focused on your goals without sacrificing your lifestyle

28.p: This wasn’t just a 30-day break — this was a reset.
A reconnection to the healthiest version of you.
Whether you choose to continue alcohol-free or simply become more mindful with your choices, one thing is clear:
That’s something to be proud of.
So take a deep breath, reflect on how far you’ve come, and carry this momentum forward — wherever your journey takes you next.
